hook: They asked me to **submit an affidavit.** What is that?
hook_q: What is an affidavit and when do I need one?

slides.title: A **sworn statement** of facts.
slides.body: An affidavit is a statement of facts that you swear or affirm before an authorised person, who administers the oath. The person making it is called the deponent.

slides.title: Who can **swear you in?**
list: A Commissioner of Oaths appointed by a High Court, Sessions Court or another empowered court
slides.ref: CPC 1908 · Sec 139 · BNSS 2023 · Sec 333(1) · Notaries Act 1952 · Sec 8(1)(e)

slides.title: Stick to **what you know.**
slides.body: Confine it to facts you can prove from your own knowledge. If you also state what you believe, keep it separate and give the grounds for that belief.
slides.note: civil: belief only on interlocutory applications
slides.ref: BNSS 2023 · Sec 333(2) · CPC 1908 · Order XIX Rule 3

slides.title: When courts **use affidavits.**
list: Examination-in-chief of a witness in civil cases
Proving particular facts, if the court orders
slides.ref: CPC 1908 · Order XVIII Rule 4, Order XIX Rules 1, 2 · BNSS 2023 · Sec 332(1)

slides.title: You can be **cross-examined.**
slides.body: When evidence is given by affidavit on an application, the court may, at either party's request, order the deponent to attend for cross-examination.
slides.ref: Code of Civil Procedure 1908 · Order XIX Rule 2

slides.title: Government form? **Self-certification** may do.
slides.body: The Centre asked all Union Ministries, Departments and State Governments to provide for self-certification of documents in place of affidavits. Originals are produced at the final stage.
slides.note: not where a law requires one

sources: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 – Section 139; Order XVIII Rule 4; Order XIX Rules 1–3
Prime Minister's Office (pmindia.gov.in) – self-certification in place of affidavits
caption:
Asked to submit an affidavit? Here's what it is. 👇

1️⃣ An affidavit is a statement of facts you swear or affirm before an authorised person
2️⃣ The oath can be given by a court or Magistrate, a notary, or a Commissioner of Oaths appointed by a court
3️⃣ Stick to facts you know yourself. State any belief separately, with its grounds
4️⃣ In civil cases, a witness's examination-in-chief is on affidavit
5️⃣ The court can call the deponent for cross-examination
6️⃣ The Centre has asked Ministries and State Governments to allow self-certification in place of affidavits

Source: CPC, 1908 (Sec 139; Order XVIII Rule 4; Order XIX); BNSS, 2023 (Sec 332, 333); Notaries Act, 1952 (Sec 8); PMO
